That which he expects and requires from his servants is that they be ready to open to him immediately, whenever he comes ( v. 36 ), that is, that they be in a frame fit to receive him, or rather to be received by him; that they be found as his servants, in the posture that becomes them, with their loins girded about, alluding to the servants that are ready to go whither their master sends them, and do what their master bids them, having their long garments tucked up (which otherwise would hang about them, and hinder them), and their lights burning, with which to light their master into the house, and up to his chamber. 5. Those servants will be happy who shall be found ready, and in a good frame, when their Lord shall come ( v. 37 ): Blessed are those servants who, after having waited long, continue in a waiting frame, until the hour that their Lord comes, and are then found awake and aware of his first approach, of his first knock; and again ( v. 38 ): Blessed are those servants, for then will be the time of their preferment. Here is such an instance of honour done them as is scarcely to be found among men: He will make them sit down to meat, and will serve them. For the bridegroom to wait upon his bride at table is not uncommon, but to wait upon his servants is not the manner of men; yet Jesus Christ was among his disciples as one that served, and did once, to show his condescension, gird himself, and serve them, when he washed their feet ( John xiii. 4, 5 ); it signified the joy with which they shall be received into the other world by the Lord Jesus, who is gone before, to prepare for them, and has told them that his Father will honour them, John xii. 26 . 6. We are therefore kept at uncertainty concerning the precise time of his coming that we may be always ready; for it is no thanks to a man to be ready for an attack, if he know beforehand just the time when it will be made: The good man of the house, if he had known what hour the thief would have come, though he were ever so careless a man, would yet have watched, and have frightened away the thieves, v. 39 . But we do not know at what hour the alarm will be given us, and therefore are concerned to watch at all tines, and never to be off our guard. Or this may intimate the miserable case of those who are careless and unbelieving in this great matter. If the good man of the house had had notice of his danger of being robbed such a night, he would have sat up, and saved his house; but we have notice of the day of the Lord's coming, as a thief in the night, to the confusion and ruin of all secure sinners, and yet do not thus watch. If men will take such care of their houses, O let us be thus wise for our souls: Be ye therefore ready also, as ready as the good man of the house would be if he knew what hour the thief would come.

But, if your hearts be set upon the earth and the things of it, it is to be feared that you have your treasure and portion in it, and are undone when you leave it. III. He charges them to get ready, and to keep in a readiness for Christ's coming, when all those who have laid up their treasure in heaven shall enter upon the enjoyment of it, v. 35 , &c. 1. Christ is our Master, and we are his servants, not only working servants, but waiting servants, servants that are to do him honour, in waiting on him, and attending his motions: If any man serve me, let him follow me. Follow the Lamb whithersoever he goes. But that is not all: they must do him honour in waiting for him, and expecting his return. We must be as men that wait for their Lord, that sit up late while he stays out late, to be ready to receive him. 2. Christ our Master, though now gone from us, will return again, return from the wedding, from solemnizing the nuptials abroad, to complete them at home. Christ's servants are now in a state of expectation, looking for their Master's glorious appearing, and doing every thing with an eye to that, and in order to that. He will come to take cognizance of his servants, and, that being a critical day, they shall either stay with him or be turned out of doors, according as they are found in that day. 3. The time of our Master's return is uncertain; it will be in the night, it will be far in the night, when he has long deferred his coming, and when many have done looking for him; in the second watch, just before midnight, or in the third watch, next after midnight, v. 38 . His coming to us, at our death, is uncertain, and to many it will be a great surprise; for the Son of Man cometh at an hour that ye think not ( v. 40 ), without giving notice beforehand. This bespeaks not only the uncertainty of the time of his coming, but the prevailing security of the greatest part of men, who are unthinking, and altogether regardless of the notices given them, so that, whenever he comes, it is in an hour that they think not. 4. That which he expects and requires from his servants is that they be ready to open to him immediately, whenever he comes ( v. 36 ), that is, that they be in a frame fit to receive him, or rather to be received by him; that they be found as his servants, in the posture that becomes them, with their loins girded about, alluding to the servants that are ready to go whither their master sends them, and do what their master bids them, having their long garments tucked up (which otherwise would hang about them, and hinder them), and their lights burning, with which to light their master into the house, and up to his chamber. 5. Those servants will be happy who shall be found ready, and in a good frame, when their Lord shall come ( v. 37 ): Blessed are those servants who, after having waited long, continue in a waiting frame, until the hour that their Lord comes, and are then found awake and aware of his first approach, of his first knock; and again ( v. 38 ): Blessed are those servants, for then will be the time of their preferment. Here is such an instance of honour done them as is scarcely to be found among men: He will make them sit down to meat, and will serve them. For the bridegroom to wait upon his bride at table is not uncommon, but to wait upon his servants is not the manner of men; yet Jesus Christ was among his disciples as one that served, and did once, to show his condescension, gird himself, and serve them, when he washed their feet ( John xiii. 4, 5 ); it signified the joy with which they shall be received into the other world by the Lord Jesus, who is gone before, to prepare for them, and has told them that his Father will honour them, John xii. 26 . 6. We are therefore kept at uncertainty concerning the precise time of his coming that we may be always ready; for it is no thanks to a man to be ready for an attack, if he know beforehand just the time when it will be made: The good man of the house, if he had known what hour the thief would have come, though he were ever so careless a man, would yet have watched, and have frightened away the thieves, v. 39 . But we do not know at what hour the alarm will be given us, and therefore are concerned to watch at all tines, and never to be off our guard. Or this may intimate the miserable case of those who are careless and unbelieving in this great matter. If the good man of the house had had notice of his danger of being robbed such a night, he would have sat up, and saved his house; but we have notice of the day of the Lord's coming, as a thief in the night, to the confusion and ruin of all secure sinners, and yet do not thus watch. If men will take such care of their houses, O let us be thus wise for our souls: Be ye therefore ready also, as ready as the good man of the house would be if he knew what hour the thief would come.

entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen25922" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Vigilance and Exertion Inculcated.</title> <div sID="gen25923" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">41</hi> Then Peter said unto him, Lord, speakest thou this parable unto us, or even to all? <hi type="super">42</hi> And the Lord said, Who then is that faithful and wise steward, whom <hi type="italic">his</hi> lord shall make ruler over his household, to give <hi type="italic">them their</hi> portion of meat in due season? <hi type="super">43</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">is</hi> that servant, whom his lord when he cometh shall find so doing. <hi type="super">44</hi> Of a truth I say unto you, that he will make him ruler over all that he hath. <hi type="super">45</hi> But and if that servant say in his heart, My lord delayeth his coming; and shall begin to beat the menservants and maidens, and to eat and drink, and to be drunken; 46 The lord of that servant will come in a day when he looketh not for <hi type="italic">him,</hi> and at a hour when he is not aware, and will cut him in sunder, and will appoint him his portion with the unbelievers. <hi type="super">47</hi> And that servant, which knew his lord's will, and prepared not <hi type="italic">himself,</hi> neither did according to his will, shall be beaten with many <hi type="italic">stripes.</hi> <hi type="super">48</hi> But he that knew not, and did commit things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with few <hi type="italic">stripes.</hi> For unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required: and to whom men have committed much, of him they will ask the more. <hi type="super">49</hi> I am come to send fire on the earth; and what will I, if it be already kindled? <hi type="super">50</hi> But I have a baptism to be baptized with; and how am I straitened till it be accomplished! <hi type="super">51</hi> Suppose ye that I am come to give peace on earth? I tell you, Nay; but rather division: <hi type="super">52</hi> For from henceforth there shall be five in one house divided, three against two, and two against three. <hi type="super">53</hi> The father shall be divided against the son, and the son against the father; the mother against the daughter, and the daughter against the mother; the mother in law against her daughter in law, and the daughter in law against her mother in law. <div eID="gen25923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25924" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. Peter's question, which he put to Christ upon occasion of the foregoing parable (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.41">v. 41</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Lord, speakest thou this parable to us</hi> that are thy constant followers, to us that are ministers, <hi type="italic">or also to all</hi> that come to be taught by thee, to all the hearers, and in them to all Christians?" Peter was now, as often, spokesman for the disciples. We have reason to bless God that there are some such forward men, that have a gift of utterance; let those that are such take heed of being proud. Now Peter desires Christ to explain himself, and to direct the arrow of the foregoing parable to the mark he intended. He calls it a <hi type="italic">parable,</hi> because it was not only figurative, but weighty, solid, and instructive. Lord, said Peter, was it intended for <hi type="italic">us,</hi> or for <hi type="italic">all?</hi> To this Christ gives a direct answer (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.37">Mark xiii. 37</reference>): <hi type="italic">What I say unto you, I say unto all.</hi> Yet here he seems to show that the apostles were primarily concerned in it. Note, We are all concerned to take to ourselves what Christ in his word designs for us, and to enquire accordingly concerning it: <hi type="italic">Speakest thou this to us?</hi> To me? Speak, Lord, for thy servant hears. Doth this word belong to me? Speak it to <hi type="italic">my heart.</hi> <div eID="gen25924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25925" type="x-p"/> II. Christ's reply to this question, directed to Peter and the rest of the disciples. If what Christ had said before did not so peculiarly concern them, but in common with other Christians, who must all watch and pray for Christ's coming, <hi type="italic">as his servants,</hi> yet this that follows is peculiarly adapted to ministers, who are the <hi type="italic">stewards</hi> in Christ's house. Now our Lord Jesus here tells them, <div eID="gen25925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25926" type="x-p"/> 1. What was their <hi type="italic">duty as stewards,</hi> and what the <hi type="italic">trust</hi> committed to them. (1.) They are made <hi type="italic">rulers of God's household,</hi> under Christ, whose own the house is; ministers derive an authority from Christ to preach the gospel, and to administer the ordinances of Christ, and apply the seals of the covenant of grace. (2.) Their business is to give God's children and servants <hi type="italic">their portion of meat,</hi> that which is proper for them and allotted to them; convictions and comfort to those to whom they respectively belong. <hi type="italic">Suum cuique</hi>—<hi type="italic">to every one his own.</hi> This is <hi type="italic">rightly to divide the word of truth,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.15">2 Tim. ii. 15</reference>. (3.) To give it to them <hi type="italic">in due season,</hi> at that time and in that way which are most suitable to the temper and condition of those that are to be fed; a word <hi type="italic">in season</hi> to him <hi type="italic">that is weary.</hi> (4.) Herein they must approve themselves <hi type="italic">faithful</hi> and <hi type="italic">wise; faithful</hi> to their Master, by whom this great trust is reposed in them, and faithful to their fellow-servants, for whose benefit they are put in trust; and <hi type="italic">wise</hi> to improve an opportunity of doing honour to their Master, and service in the family. Ministers must be both <hi type="italic">skilful</hi> and <hi type="italic">faithful.</hi> <div eID="gen25926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25927" type="x-p"/> 2. What would be their happiness if they approved themselves faithful and wise (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.43">v. 43</reference>): <hi type="italic">Blessed is that servant,</hi> (1.) That is <hi type="italic">doing,</hi> and is not idle, nor indulgent of his ease; even the rulers of the household must be <hi type="italic">doing,</hi> and make themselves <hi type="italic">servants of all.</hi> (2.) That is <hi type="italic">so</hi> doing, doing as he should be, giving them their <hi type="italic">portion of meat,</hi> by public preaching and personal application. (3.) That is <hi type="italic">found</hi> so doing when his Lord comes; that perseveres to the end, notwithstanding the difficulties he may meet with in the way. Now his happiness is illustrated by the preferment of a steward that has approved himself within a lower and narrower degree of service; he shall be preferred to a larger and higher (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.44">v. 44</reference>): <hi type="italic">He will make him ruler over all that he has,</hi> which was Joseph's preferment in Pharaoh's court. Note, Ministers that obtain mercy of the Lord to be faithful shall obtain further mercy to be abundantly rewarded for their faithfulness in the day of the Lord. <div eID="gen25927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25928" type="x-p"/> 3. What a dreadful reckoning there would be if they were treacherous and unfaithful, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.45-Luke.12.46">v. 45, 46</reference>. If that servant begin to be quarrelsome and profane, he shall be called to an account, and severely punished. We had all this before in Matthew, and therefore shall here only observe, (1.) Our looking upon Christ's second coming as a thing at a distance is the cause of all those irregularities which render the thought of it terrible to us: <hi type="italic">He saith in his heart, My Lord delays his coming.</hi> Christ's patience is very often misinterpreted his <hi type="italic">delay,</hi> to the <hi type="italic">dis</hi>couragement of his people, and the <hi type="italic">en</hi>couragement of his enemies. (2.) The persecutors of God's people are commonly abandoned to security and sensuality; <hi type="italic">they beat their fellow-servants,</hi> and then <hi type="italic">eat and drink with the drunken,</hi> altogether unconcerned either at their own sin or their brethren's sufferings, as the king and Haman, who <hi type="italic">sat down to drink when the city Shushan was perplexed.</hi> Thus they drink, to drown the clamours of their own consciences, and baffle them, which would otherwise fly in their faces. (3.) Death and judgment will be very terrible to all wicked people, but especially to wicked ministers. It will be a surprise to them: <hi type="italic">At an hour when they are not aware.</hi> It will be the determining of them to endless misery; they shall be cut in sunder, and have their portion assigned them with <hi type="italic">the unbelievers.</hi> <div eID="gen25928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25929" type="x-p"/> 4. What an aggravation it would be of their sin and punishment that they knew their duty, and did not do it (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.47-Luke.12.48">v. 47, 48</reference>): <hi type="italic">That servant that knew his lord's will, and did it not, shall be beaten with many stripes,</hi> shall fall under a sorer punishment; and <hi type="italic">he that knew not shall be beaten with few stripes,</hi> his punishment shall, in consideration of this, be mitigated. Here seems to be an allusion to the law, which made a distinction between sins committed through ignorance, and presumptuous sins (<reference osisRef="Lev.5.15 Num.15.29-Num.15.30">Lev. v. 15, &c.; Num. xv. 29, 30</reference>), as also to another law concerning the number of stripes given to a malefactor, to be according to the nature of the crime, <reference osisRef="Deut.25.2-Deut.25.3">Deut. xxv. 2, 3</reference>. Now, (1.) Ignorance of our duty is an extenuation of sin. He <hi type="italic">that knew not his lord's will,</hi> through carelessness and neglect, and his not having such opportunities as some others had of coming to the knowledge of it, and <hi type="italic">did things worthy of stripes,</hi> he shall <hi type="italic">be beaten,</hi> because he might have known his duty better, but <hi type="italic">with few stripes;</hi> his ignorance excuses in part, but not wholly. Thus <hi type="italic">through ignorance</hi> the Jews put Christ to death (<reference osisRef="Acts.3.17">Acts iii. 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.8">1 Cor. ii. 8</reference>), and Christ pleaded that ignorance in their excuse: <hi type="italic">They know not what they do.</hi> (2.) The knowledge of our duty is an aggravation of our sin: <hi type="italic">That servant that knew his lord's will,</hi> and yet did his own will, shall be <hi type="italic">beaten with many stripes.</hi> God will justly inflict more upon him for abusing the means of knowledge he afforded him, which others would have made a better use of, because it argues a great degree of wilfulness and contempt to sin against knowledge; of how much sorer punishment then shall they be thought worthy, besides the many stripes that their own consciences will give them! Son, remember. Here is a good reason for this added: <hi type="italic">To whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required,</hi> especially when it is <hi type="italic">committed</hi> as a trust he is to account for. Those have greater capacities of mind than others, more knowledge and learning, more acquaintance and converse with the scriptures, to them <hi type="italic">much is given,</hi> and their account will be accordingly. <div eID="gen25929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25930" type="x-p"/> III. A further discourse concerning his own sufferings, which he expected, and concerning the sufferings of his followers, which he would have them also to live in expectation of. In general (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.49">v. 49</reference>): <hi type="italic">I am come to send fire on the earth.</hi> By this some understand the preaching of the gospel, and the pouring out of the Spirit, holy fire; this Christ came to send with a commission to refine the world, to purge away its dross, to burn up its chaff, and it was <hi type="italic">already kindled.</hi> The gospel was begun to be preached; some prefaces there were to the pouring out of the Spirit. Christ baptized with the Holy Ghost and with fire; this Spirit descended in fiery tongues. But, by what follows, it seems rather to be understood of the fire of <hi type="italic">persecution.</hi> Christ is not the Author of it, as it is the sin of the incendiaries, the <hi type="italic">persecutors;</hi> but he <hi type="italic">permits</hi> it, nay, he <hi type="italic">commissions</hi> it, as a <hi type="italic">refining</hi> fire for the <hi type="italic">trial</hi> of the <hi type="italic">persecuted.</hi> This fire was <hi type="italic">already kindled</hi> in the enmity of the carnal Jews to Christ and his followers. "<hi type="italic">What will I that it may presently be kindled? What thou doest, do quickly. If it be already kindled, what will I?</hi> Shall I wait the <hi type="italic">quenching</hi> of it? No, for it must fasten upon myself, and upon all, and glory will redound to God from it." <div eID="gen25930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25931" type="x-p"/> 1. He must himself suffer many things; he must pass through this fire that was already kindled (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.50">v. 50</reference>): <hi type="italic">I have a baptism to be baptized with.</hi> Afflictions are compared both to <hi type="italic">fire</hi> and <hi type="italic">water,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.66.12">Ps. lxvi. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.69.1-Ps.69.2">lxix. 1, 2</reference>. Christ's sufferings were both. He calls them a <hi type="italic">baptism</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.20.22">Matt. xx. 22</reference>); for he was watered or sprinkled with them, as Israel was baptized <hi type="italic">in the cloud,</hi> and dipped into them, as Israel was baptized <hi type="italic">in the sea,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.2">1 Cor. x. 2</reference>. He must be sprinkled with his own blood, and with the blood of his enemies, <reference osisRef="Isa.63.3">Isa. lxiii. 3</reference>. See here, (1.) Christ's <hi type="italic">foresight</hi> of his sufferings; he knew what he was to undergo, and the necessity of undergoing it: <hi type="italic">I am to be baptized with a baptism.</hi> He calls his sufferings by a name that <hi type="italic">mitigates</hi> them; it is a baptism, not a deluge; I must be <hi type="italic">dipped</hi> in them, not <hi type="italic">drowned</hi> in them; and by a name that <hi type="italic">sanctifies</hi> them, for baptism is a name that <hi type="italic">sanctifies</hi> them, for baptism is a sacred rite. Christ in his sufferings <hi type="italic">devoted</hi> himself to his Father's honour, and <hi type="italic">consecrated</hi> himself a priest for evermore, <reference osisRef="Heb.7.27-Heb.7.28">Heb. vii. 27, 28</reference>. (2.) Christ's <hi type="italic">forwardness</hi> to his sufferings: <hi type="italic">How am I straitened till it be accomplished!</hi> He longed for the time when he should suffer and die, having an eye to the glorious issue of his sufferings. It is an allusion to a woman in travail, that is <hi type="italic">pained to be delivered,</hi> and welcomes her pains, because they hasten the birth of the child, and wishes them sharp and strong, that the <hi type="italic">work</hi> may be <hi type="italic">cut short.</hi> Christ's sufferings were the <hi type="italic">travail of his soul,</hi> which he cheerfully underwent, in hope that he should by them <hi type="italic">see his seed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.53.10-Isa.53.11">Isa. liii. 10, 11</reference>. So much was his heart set upon the redemption and salvation of man. <div eID="gen25931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25932" type="x-p"/> 2. He tells those about him that they also must bear with hardships and difficulties (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.51">v. 51</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Suppose ye that I came to give peace on earth,</hi> to give you a peaceable possession of the earth, and outward prosperity on the earth?" It is intimated that they were ready to entertain such a thought as this, nay, that they went upon this supposition, that the gospel would meet with a <hi type="italic">universal</hi> welcome, that people <hi type="italic">unanimously</hi> embrace it, and would therefore study to make the preachers of it <hi type="italic">easy</hi> and <hi type="italic">great,</hi> that Christ, if he did not give them <hi type="italic">pomp</hi> and <hi type="italic">power,</hi> would at least give them <hi type="italic">peace;</hi> and herein they were encouraged by divers passages of the Old Testament, which speak of the peace of the Messiah's kingdom, which they were willing to understand of external peace. "But," saith Christ, "you will be mistaken, the event will declare the contrary, and therefore do not flatter yourselves into a fool's paradise. You will find," <div eID="gen25932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25933" type="x-p"/> (1.) "That the effect of the preaching of the gospel will be <hi type="italic">division.</hi>" Not but that the design of the gospel and its proper tendency are to unite the children of men to one another, to knit them together in holy love, and, if all would receive it, this would be the effect of it; but there being multitudes that not only will not receive it, but oppose it, and have their corruptions exasperated by it, and are enraged at those that do receive it, it proves, though not the <hi type="italic">cause</hi> yet the <hi type="italic">occasion</hi> of <hi type="italic">division.</hi> While <hi type="italic">the strong man armed kept his palace,</hi> in the Gentile world, <hi type="italic">his goods were at peace;</hi> all was quiet, for all went one way, the sects of philosophers agreed well enough, so did the worshippers of different deities; but when the gospel was preached, and many were enlightened by it, and turned from the power of Satan to God, then there was a disturbance, <hi type="italic">a noise and a shaking,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.7">Ezek. xxxvii. 7</reference>. Some <hi type="italic">distinguished</hi> themselves by embracing the gospel, and others were angry that they did so. Yea, and among them that received the gospel there would be different sentiments in minor things, which would occasion <hi type="italic">division;</hi> and Christ permits it for holy ends (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.18">1 Cor. xi. 18</reference>), that Christians may learn and practise mutual forbearance, <reference osisRef="Rom.14.1-Rom.14.2">Rom. xiv. 1, 2</reference>. <div eID="gen25933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25934" type="x-p"/> (2.) "That this <hi type="italic">division</hi> will reach into private families, and the preaching of the gospel will give occasion for discord among the nearest relations" (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.53">v. 53</reference>): <hi type="italic">The father shall be divided against the son, and the son against the father,</hi> when the one turns Christian and the other does not; for the one that does turn Christian will be zealous by arguments and endearments to turn the other too, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.16">1 Cor. vii. 16</reference>. As soon as ever Paul was converted, he <hi type="italic">disputed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.9.29">Acts ix. 29</reference>. The one that continues in unbelief will be provoked, and will hate and persecute the one that by his faith and obedience witnesses against, and condemns, his unbelief and disobedience. A spirit of bigotry and persecution will break through the strongest bonds of relation and natural affection; see <reference osisRef="Matt.10.35">Matt. x. 35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.24.7">xxiv. 7</reference>. Even <hi type="italic">mothers</hi> and <hi type="italic">daughters</hi> fall out about religion; and those that believe not are so violent and outrageous that they are ready to deliver up into the hands of the bloody persecutors those that believe, though otherwise very near and dear to them. We find in the <hi type="italic">Acts</hi> that, wherever the gospel came, <hi type="italic">persecution</hi> was <hi type="italic">stirred up;</hi> it was <hi type="italic">every where spoken against,</hi> and there was <hi type="italic">no small stir about that way.</hi> Therefore let not the disciples of Christ promise themselves <hi type="italic">peace upon earth,</hi> for they are sent forth <hi type="italic">as sheep in the midst of wolves.</hi>
entries.content_plain: Vigilance and Exertion Inculcated. 41 Then Peter said unto him, Lord, speakest thou this parable unto us, or even to all? 42 And the Lord said, Who then is that faithful and wise steward, whom his lord shall make ruler over his household, to give them their portion of meat in due season? 43 Blessed is that servant, whom his lord when he cometh shall find so doing. 44 Of a truth I say unto you, that he will make him ruler over all that he hath. 45 But and if that servant say in his heart, My lord delayeth his coming; and shall begin to beat the menservants and maidens, and to eat and drink, and to be drunken; 46 The lord of that servant will come in a day when he looketh not for him, and at a hour when he is not aware, and will cut him in sunder, and will appoint him his portion with the unbelievers. 47 And that servant, which knew his lord's will, and prepared not himself, neither did according to his will, shall be beaten with many stripes. 48 But he that knew not, and did commit things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with few stripes. For unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required: and to whom men have committed much, of him they will ask the more. 49 I am come to send fire on the earth; and what will I, if it be already kindled? 50 But I have a baptism to be baptized with; and how am I straitened till it be accomplished! 51 Suppose ye that I am come to give peace on earth? I tell you, Nay; but rather division: 52 For from henceforth there shall be five in one house divided, three against two, and two against three. 53 The father shall be divided against the son, and the son against the father; the mother against the daughter, and the daughter against the mother; the mother in law against her daughter in law, and the daughter in law against her mother in law. Here is, I. Peter's question, which he put to Christ upon occasion of the foregoing parable ( v. 41 ): " Lord, speakest thou this parable to us that are thy constant followers, to us that are ministers, or also to all that come to be taught by thee, to all the hearers, and in them to all Christians?" Doth this word belong to me? Speak it to my heart. II. Christ's reply to this question, directed to Peter and the rest of the disciples. If what Christ had said before did not so peculiarly concern them, but in common with other Christians, who must all watch and pray for Christ's coming, as his servants, yet this that follows is peculiarly adapted to ministers, who are the stewards in Christ's house. They are made rulers of God's household, under Christ, whose own the house is; ministers derive an authority from Christ to preach the gospel, and to administer the ordinances of Christ, and apply the seals of the covenant of grace. entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen25934" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Reconciliation to God.</title> <div sID="gen25935" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">54</hi> And he said also to the people, When ye see a cloud rise out of the west, straightway ye say, There cometh a shower; and so it is. <hi type="super">55</hi> And when <hi type="italic">ye see</hi> the south wind blow, ye say, There will be heat; and it cometh to pass. 56 <hi type="italic">Ye</hi> hypocrites, ye can discern the face of the sky and of the earth; but how is it that ye do not discern this time? 57 Yea, and why even of yourselves judge ye not what is right? <hi type="super">58</hi> When thou goest with thine adversary to the magistrate, <hi type="italic">as thou art</hi> in the way, give diligence that thou mayest be delivered from him; lest he hale thee to the judge, and the judge deliver thee to the officer, and the officer cast thee into prison. <hi type="super">59</hi> I tell thee, thou shalt not depart thence, till thou hast paid the very last mite. <div eID="gen25935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25936" type="x-p"/> Having given his disciples <hi type="italic">their</hi> lesson in the foregoing verses, here Christ turns to <hi type="italic">the people,</hi> and gives them <hi type="italic">theirs,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.12.54">v. 54</reference>. He <hi type="italic">said also to the people:</hi> he preached <hi type="italic">ad populum—to the people,</hi> as well as <hi type="italic">ad clerum—to the clergy.</hi> In general, he would have them be as wise in the affairs of their souls as they are in their outward affairs. Two things he specifies:— <div eID="gen25936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25937" type="x-p"/> I. Let them learn to <hi type="italic">discern the way of God towards them,</hi> that they may <hi type="italic">prepare</hi> accordingly. They were <hi type="italic">weather-wise,</hi> and by observing the winds and clouds could foresee when there would be <hi type="italic">rain</hi> and when there would be <hi type="italic">hot weather</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.54-Luke.12.55">v. 54, 55</reference>); and, according as they foresaw the weather would be, they either housed their hay and corn, or threw it abroad, and equipped themselves for a journey? Even in regard to changes of the weather God gives warning to us what is coming, and art has improved the notices of nature in weather-glasses. The prognostications here referred to had their origin in repeated observations upon the chain of causes: from what <hi type="italic">has been</hi> we conjecture what <hi type="italic">will be.</hi> See the benefit of experience; by <hi type="italic">taking notice</hi> we may come to <hi type="italic">give notice.</hi> Whose is wise will <hi type="italic">observe</hi> and <hi type="italic">learn.</hi> See now. <div eID="gen25937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25938" type="x-p"/> 1. The particulars of the presages: "<hi type="italic">When you see a cloud arising out of the west</hi>" (the Hebrew would say, <hi type="italic">out of the sea</hi>), "perhaps it is at first <hi type="italic">no bigger than a man's hand</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.44">1 Kings xviii. 44</reference>), but you say, There is a shower in the womb of it, and it proves so. When you <hi type="italic">observe</hi> the <hi type="italic">south wind blow,</hi> you say, <hi type="italic">There will be heat</hi>" (for the hot countries of Africa lay not far south from Judea), "and it usually <hi type="italic">comes to pass;</hi>" yet nature has not ties itself to such a track but that <hi type="italic">sometimes</hi> we are mistaken in our prognostics. <div eID="gen25938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25939" type="x-p"/> 2. The inferences from them (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.56">v. 56</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Ye hypocrites,</hi> who pretend to be wise, but really are not so, who pretend to expect the Messiah and his kingdom" (for so the generality of the Jews did) "and yet are no way disposed to receive and entertain it, <hi type="italic">how is it that you do not discern this time,</hi> that you do not discern that now is the time, according to the indications given in the Old-Testament prophecies, for the Messiah to appear, and that, according to the marks given of him, I am he? Why are you not aware that you have now an opportunity which you <hi type="italic">will not have long,</hi> and which you <hi type="italic">may never have again,</hi> of securing to yourselves an interest in the kingdom of God and the privileges of that kingdom?" <hi type="italic">Now is the accepted time,</hi> now or never. It is the folly and misery of man that he <hi type="italic">knows not his time,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.12">Eccl. ix. 12</reference>. We reckon it our wisdom in our temporal affairs to compound with those with whom we cannot contend, to agree with our adversary upon the best terms we can, before the equity be foreclosed, and we be left to the rigour of the law: " When thou goest with thine adversary to the magistrate, to whom the appeal is made, and knowest that he has an advantage against thee, and thou art in danger of being cast, thou knowest it is the most prudent course to make the matter up between yourselves; as thou art in the way, give diligence to be delivered from him, to get a discharge, lest judgment be given, and execution awarded according to law." We have by sin made God our adversary, have provoked his displeasure against us, and he has both right and might on his side; so that it is to no purpose to think of carrying on the controversy with him either at bar or in battle. Let us take hold on the arm of the Lord stretched out in this gracious offer, that we may make peace, and we shall make peace ( Isa. xxvii. 4, 5 ), for we cannot walk together till we be agreed.

navigation_sections.content_plain: In this chapter we have divers excellent discourses of our Saviour's upon various occasions, many of which are to the same purport with what we had in Matthew upon other the like occasions; for we may suppose that our Lord Jesus preached the same doctrines, and pressed the same duties, at several times, in several companies, and that one of the evangelists took them as he delivered them at one time and another at another time; and we need thus to have precept upon precept, line upon line. Here, I. Christ warns his disciples to take heed of hypocrisy, and of cowardice in professing Christianity and preaching the gospel, ver. 1-12 . II. He gives a caution against covetousness, upon occasion of a covetous motion made to him, and illustrates that caution by a parable of a rich man suddenly cut off by death in the midst of his worldly projects and hopes, ver. 13-21 . III. He encourages his disciples to cast all their care upon God, and to live easy in a dependence upon his providence, and exhorts them to make religion their main business, ver. 22-34 . IV. He stirs them up to watchfulness for their Master's coming, from the consideration of the reward of those who are then found faithful, and the punishment of those who are found unfaithful, ver. 35-48 . V. He bids them expect trouble and persecution, ver. 49-53 . VI. He warns the people to observe and improve the day of their opportunities and to make their peace with God in time, ver. 54-59 .
